title: Encapsulation
summary: Bundling state with the behavior that protects it, and why that's more than "add getters and setters" — invariants, access modifiers, and where they actually earn their keep.

slides.markdown:
**Encapsulation** means bundling an object's state with the only methods allowed to change it, so nothing outside the object can put it in a broken state. It's not "hide the fields and add getters/setters" — that pattern alone protects nothing.

This topic covers what encapsulation actually buys you: enforceable invariants, access modifiers that back them, and the specific ways people fake encapsulation while leaving the real protection out.

slides.sectionTitle: Encapsulation defined: bundling state with the behavior that protects it
slides.markdown:
**Encapsulation** is bundling an object's state together with the methods that are allowed to change it, and denying every other piece of code direct access to that state. The state isn't just packaged with behavior for convenience — the behavior exists specifically to guard rules the state must obey.

A `Thermostat` that only exposes `setTargetTemperature(int celsius)` — never a raw `targetTemperature` field — can reject `setTargetTemperature(-500)` inside that one method. Every caller, everywhere in the codebase, goes through that same check.

The test for real encapsulation: is there a rule this object enforces that would break if a caller could reach in and set the field directly? If yes, you have encapsulation; if there's no such rule, you just have private fields with pass-through methods.

slides.sectionTitle: Why public fields let callers break an object's invariants
slides.markdown:
A `public` field is a promise with no enforcement: any code anywhere can read it, and worse, write it, with zero say from the object itself. If `BankAccount.balance` is `public`, then `account.balance = -500;` is perfectly legal syntax — the language has no way to stop it.

The object's own methods can carefully protect `balance` in `withdraw()` and `deposit()`, and none of that protection matters the moment one caller, anywhere in a million-line codebase, decides to assign the field directly. One violation is enough to corrupt the object.

This is the concrete cost of skipping encapsulation: it's not a style preference, it's the difference between a rule that's enforced everywhere and a rule that's enforced nowhere, because it can always be bypassed.

slides.sectionTitle: Access modifiers: public/private/protected/package — what each actually buys you
slides.markdown:
Access modifiers are how a language lets a class draw its own boundary. **`private`** — visible only inside the class itself; the strongest guarantee, use it as the default for fields. **`public`** — visible to any code that can reach the object; reserve it for the deliberate contract you want to expose. **`protected`** — visible to the class and its subclasses, a controlled crack in the wall for inheritance (more in the Inheritance topic). **Package-private** (Java's default, no keyword) — visible to other classes in the same package, useful for tightly-coupled helper classes that shouldn't leak further.

The decision that matters: start every field `private`, and widen access only when you have a concrete reason — not "might need it later." Widening later is easy; narrowing a public field after other code depends on it is a breaking change.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: getters/setters on every field isn't automatically encapsulation
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I made every field `private` and added a `getX()`/`setX()` pair for each one, so this class is encapsulated."

**Why it's wrong:** a `setBalance(double balance) { this.balance = balance; }` setter enforces exactly nothing — it's a public field wearing a method-shaped disguise. Any caller can still set `balance` to `-500` through the setter just as freely as through a public field; the invariant is still unprotected.

**Correct model:** encapsulation is measured by what rules are enforced, not by how many fields are private. A setter earns its keep only when it validates or transforms the value (`setBalance` rejecting negatives, or exposing `deposit`/`withdraw` instead of a raw setter at all) — otherwise, delete the pointless getter/setter pair and ask what operation the object should actually expose.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an object as a capsule — what's exposed vs hidden
slides.markdown:
Picture an object as a sealed capsule: its internal state sits inside, invisible from outside, and the only way in or out is through a small, deliberate set of methods on the capsule's surface. Callers can invoke `deposit()` or `withdraw()`, but they can never reach past that surface to touch `balance` directly.

The size of that surface is a design choice — expose too much and you've built a leaky capsule with private fields in name only; expose too little and legitimate callers can't get anything done. Good encapsulation is choosing the smallest surface that still lets the object be genuinely useful.

slides.sectionTitle: Invariants: rules an object must never violate, enforced in one place
slides.markdown:
An **invariant** is a rule that must hold for every valid instance of a class, at every point after construction — "a `BankAccount`'s balance is never negative," "a `NonEmptyList` always has at least one element." Encapsulation exists to give invariants exactly one place to be enforced: inside the class's own methods.

Without encapsulation, the same rule has to be re-checked by every caller, everywhere the state is touched — and the one caller who forgets breaks the guarantee for the whole system. With it, `withdraw()` checks `amount <= balance` once, and every path that changes `balance` is forced through that check because there's no other path in.

When you design a class, write down its invariants explicitly first — they tell you exactly which methods need validation and which fields must stay private.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: encapsulating a BankAccount balance so it can never go negative
Compare: encapsulation vs abstraction — hiding implementation vs hiding complexity
slides.markdown:
These two get conflated constantly, and interviewers know it — the crisp distinction is worth having ready. Full treatment in [abstraction](abstraction).

| | Encapsulation | Abstraction |
|---|---|---|
| Question it answers | Who can touch this state, and how? | What does this expose to callers, regardless of who they are? |
| Mechanism | Access modifiers (`private`), enforced invariants | Interfaces, abstract classes, method signatures |
| Primary goal | Protect internal state from corruption | Hide unnecessary complexity behind a simple contract |
| Failure mode when missing | Invariants get violated from outside | Callers get coupled to implementation details that shouldn't matter |

**How to decide which term to use:** if the concern is "can this be set to an invalid value," that's encapsulation; if the concern is "does the caller need to know how this works internally," that's abstraction. A well-designed class usually needs both.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: leaking an internal mutable collection through a getter
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "My field is `private List<String> tags`, and I only expose it through `getTags()` — that's read-only, so it's safe."

**Why it's wrong:** `getTags()` returning the live `List` object hands the caller a direct reference to your internal state, not a copy. `account.getTags().clear();` silently empties the real list from outside the class — no setter was ever called, yet the invariant is gone, because a mutable object was leaked, not copied.

**Correct model:** return a defensive copy (`return new ArrayList<>(tags);`) or an unmodifiable view (`Collections.unmodifiableList(tags)`) from any getter that exposes a mutable collection or object. "Private field" only protects the reference itself — it says nothing about what the caller can do to the object that reference points at.
